docs.title: Feather Sample Collection Protocol
docs.text: Feather samples are the most commonly submitted sample type to SENO's avian genetics laboratory. When collected correctly, freshly plucked feathers provide reliable DNA for sexing, genetic disease screening, and species identification. This protocol covers proper plucking technique, quality control, species-specific guidance, and packaging standards.

docs.title: Why Freshly Plucked Feathers Are Essential
docs.text:
DNA quality is the single most important factor for accurate testing. Feathers must be freshly plucked — the DNA in feather samples comes exclusively from the follicle cells at the base of the feather shaft. Shed feathers found on the cage floor have desiccated follicles and will not yield viable DNA for PCR amplification.

Feather Condition Follicle Cells DNA Viability Test Reliability Freshly plucked Present (visible bulb) High > 95% first-pass success Shed (molted) Absent or degraded Very low < 10% success rate Stored > 4 weeks Drying out Declining Increased re-test probability Moldy or wet Degraded None Sample rejected

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text: Item Purpose Notes Clean paper envelope (per bird) Sample container Never use plastic bags — condensation causes mold Disposable gloves Prevent cross-contamination Change gloves between birds Sterile forceps (optional) Handle small feathers Useful for finches and budgies Permanent marker Labeling Use waterproof ink Breathable padded mailer Shipping container Protects feather follicles from crushing

docs.title: Step 1: Restrain the Bird
docs.text: Restrain the bird gently but securely. For small birds, use a towel or cupped hands. For larger birds (parrots, macaws), a second person may be needed to stabilize the head and body.

docs.title: Step 2: Identify the Collection Site
docs.text:
Select feathers from the chest or flank region. These feathers have the best follicle development and provide the highest DNA yield. Avoid wing and tail feathers — they are more painful to remove and the follicles may be damaged.

Collection Site Recommendation Rationale Chest Best choice Large, well-developed follicles; minimal stress Flank Excellent alternative Good follicle size; easy access Wing coverts Acceptable Smaller follicles; more discomfort Tail feathers Not recommended Painful; risk of follicle damage or bleeding

docs.title: Step 3: Pluck the Feather
docs.text:
1. Grasp the feather close to the skin using thumb and forefinger
  2. Pull firmly and quickly in the direction of feather growth
  3. Inspect the follicle — a small tissue bulb should be visible at the feather base
  4. If the bulb is absent or appears dry, the feather was shed — discard and collect another

docs.title: Step 4: Collect the Required Number of Feathers
docs.text: Bird Size Examples Feathers Required Recommended Location Small Budgie, finch, canary, parrotlet 5–7 Chest or flank Medium Conure, lovebird, cockatiel, pigeon 3–5 Chest or flank Large Macaw, cockatoo, African grey, Amazon 2–3 Chest Extra-large Emu, ostrich, swan 1–2 Chest or flank

docs.title: Step 5: Place Feathers into Envelope
docs.text:
• Open the paper envelope and drop the feathers directly inside
  • Do not touch the feather base with fingers — oils from skin can contaminate the sample
  • Fold the envelope flap but do not seal until ready to ship (air circulation prevents mold)
  • Label the envelope immediately with bird ID, collection date, species, and owner name

docs.title: Step 6: Verify Sample Quality
docs.text:
Before finishing the collection, confirm the following quality criteria:

  • [ ] 3–7 feathers collected (per species guidance above)
  • [ ] Follicle bulbs visible on all feathers
  • [ ] No visible blood, fecal material, or dirt on feather shafts
  • [ ] Feathers are dry and intact
  • [ ] Envelope is labeled with bird ID and date
  • [ ] Gloves changed between birds (if collecting from multiple birds)

docs.title: Critical Rules Table
docs.text: ✅ Do ❌ Don't Pluck fresh feathers only — verify follicle bulb is present Use shed feathers from the cage floor or perch Label each bird's envelope immediately after collection Mix multiple birds' feathers in one envelope Use breathable paper envelopes Seal feathers in plastic bags (condensation → mold) Store at room temperature (15–25°C) in a dry, dark place Refrigerate or freeze feathers Ship within 2–4 weeks of collection Expose to extreme heat, direct sunlight, or humidity Collect from chest or flank Pull wing or tail feathers unnecessarily Change gloves between birds Handle multiple birds without glove changes

docs.title: Psittacines (Parrots, Macaws, Cockatoos)
docs.text: Large psittacines have strong, well-developed chest feathers. Collect 2–3 feathers from the upper chest. For macaws, the feathers are thick — ensure the follicle bulb is intact after plucking.

docs.title: Passerines (Finches, Canaries, Sparrows)
docs.text: These small birds have delicate skin and fine feathers. Use sterile forceps for better control. Collect 5–7 breast feathers. Watch for signs of stress and stop if the bird shows distress.

docs.title: Columbiformes (Pigeons, Doves)
docs.text: Pigeons have loosely attached chest feathers that pluck easily. Collect 3–5 feathers. Pigeon feathers may have less visible follicle tissue — inspect closely and consider a blood or swab sample if follicle quality is poor.

docs.title: Galliformes (Chickens, Turkeys, Quail)
docs.text: These birds have dense feather coverage. Collect 3–5 feathers from the breast or flank. Avoid blood feathers (newly forming feathers with a blood-filled shaft).

docs.title: Raptors (Hawks, Falcons, Owls)
docs.text: Raptor feathers are tightly attached and require more force to pluck. Collect 2–3 chest feathers. For sensitive species, consider a blood or swab sample as an alternative.

docs.title: Waterfowl (Ducks, Geese, Swans)
docs.text: Waterfowl have waterproof feathers with oil glands. Oil on the feather shaft may interfere with PCR — wipe the shaft gently with a clean tissue before placing in the envelope. Collect 2–3 flank feathers.

docs.title: Packaging for Shipment
docs.text: Step Action Key Point 1 Place labeled paper envelope(s) in a padded mailer Do not add extra packaging material that could crush follicles 2 Include the SENO submission form Ensure bird ID on envelope matches the form 3 Seal the padded mailer Use tamper-evident tape if crossing borders 4 Attach the shipping label Address to SENO's receiving department 5 Ship Monday–Wednesday Avoid weekend holds at customs or courier facilities

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Likely Cause Solution No follicle bulb visible Feather was shed or molt-stage Re-pluck with firm, quick pull Feather base is bloody Cut a blood feather Apply pressure; avoid bloody feathers Feathers appear moldy Stored in plastic or high humidity Switch to paper envelopes; include desiccant Low DNA yield Too few feathers or old sample Re-collect 5–7 fresh feathers Bird shows stress during collection Restraint or technique too rough Stop, let bird rest, try again with gentler restraint

docs.title: Why Paper Envelopes Are Mandatory
docs.text:
Feather follicles contain viable cells that need to breathe. Plastic bags trap residual moisture from the feather or environment, creating a microclimate that promotes mold and bacterial growth. Mold degrades DNA and renders the sample untestable. Paper envelopes allow air circulation while keeping the feathers contained.

Container Suitability Reason Paper envelope ✅ Excellent Breathable, lightweight, protects follicles Cardboard box ✅ Good with envelope inside Adds structural protection for shipping Plastic bag ❌ Never use Traps moisture, causes mold in 24–48 hours Glass vial ❌ Not recommended Crushes follicles; no airflow Aluminum foil ❌ Avoid Traps moisture; tears easily

docs.title: International Sample Shipping Guide — Avian DNA Testing
docs.text: canonical: https://aviantestpro.com/knowledge/sample-guide/international-shipping

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: SENO regularly receives international samples from breeders, pet shops, veterinary clinics, and distributors worldwide. Our team provides full shipping guidance and customs clearance documentation support. This guide covers packaging, documentation, CITES compliance, carrier selection, and country-specific restrictions.

docs.title: General Timeline
docs.text: Step Estimated Duration Notes Sample collection to dispatch 1 day Collect samples per guidelines; label clearly International shipping 3–5 business days Courier (DHL, FedEx, UPS — door-to-door) Customs processing 2–3 business days Varies by country; pre-clearance documentation helps Laboratory testing 1–2 business days Most assays completed within 48 h of receipt Reporting 1 business day Results delivered via email or online portal Total turnaround 7–10 business days From dispatch to result receipt

docs.title: Step 1: Sample Collection and Preparation
docs.text: Sample Type Collection Instructions Minimum Required Feathers Pluck 3–5 feathers with intact follicles (visible bulb at base); place in clean paper envelope; label with bird ID 3 feathers with visible follicles Oral / cloacal swab Swab target area for 10–15 seconds; place swab into tube with nucleic acid stabilization solution; seal tightly 1 swab per test (2 for full panel) Blood (FTA card) Apply 2–3 drops of blood to FTA card circle; air-dry completely (30–60 min) before sealing 1 circle with ≥ 1 cm diameter spot Blood (liquid EDTA) Collect in EDTA tube (not heparin); fill tube to at least 1/3 volume; mix gently 100–200 µL whole blood

docs.title: Step 2: Primary Packaging
docs.text:
1. Feathers: Paper envelope (never plastic — plastic causes condensation and mold) → seal → place in ziplock bag
  2. Swabs: Verify tube cap is fully tightened → wrap cap junction with parafilm (optional but recommended) → place in leak-proof secondary container
  3. Liquid blood: EDTA tube with tight cap → wrap with absorbent material (paper towel) → place in secondary leak-proof tube
  4. FTA card: Allow card to dry completely → place in original sleeve → seal in ziplock bag

docs.title: Step 3: Secondary Packaging
docs.text:
All sample types must be enclosed in a secondary, leak-proof container:

Material Specification Absorbent material Sufficient to absorb entire contents of primary container (2× volume) Secondary container Watertight plastic bag or rigid plastic tube Cushioning Bubble wrap or foam, minimum 2 cm on all sides

docs.title: Step 4: Outer Packaging
docs.text:
1. Use a sturdy corrugated cardboard box or padded courier envelope
  2. Label outer package as: "Biological Specimen, Category B" (UN3373) — required for swabs and blood
  3. Include the following inside the package:
  4. Completed submission form
  5. Commercial invoice (2 copies)
  6. Packing list
  7. Letter of explanation (provided by SENO)

docs.title: Step 5: Documentation
docs.text:
Attach securely to the outside of the package:

  • [ ] Courier airway bill (completed)
  • [ ] UN3374 label (if applicable — liquid samples only)
  • [ ] "This side up" directional arrows (if liquid)
  • [ ] Shipper's declaration (contact SENO for template)
  • [ ] Customs declaration form
  • [ ] CITES permit (if required — see below)

docs.title: Step 6: Dispatch
docs.text: Courier Recommended For Tracking Notes DHL All destinations (best global coverage) Yes Most SENO clients use DHL Express FedEx Americas, Europe Yes Good alternative where DHL unavailable UPS Europe, Asia-Pacific Yes Competitive transit times EMS Budget option, available in most countries Yes Slower (5–10 business days)

docs.title: CITES Requirements
docs.text:
The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) regulates transport of samples from listed species.

CITES Appendix Species Examples Permit Required SENO Advice Appendix I Spix's Macaw, Philippine Eagle, some cockatoo species Both export AND import permit required Contact SENO before collecting — significant lead time needed (2–6 months) Appendix II Most parrots (African Grey, Amazon, Macaw, Cockatoo), some pigeon species Export permit from country of origin required SENO provides CITES declaration support; allow 4–8 weeks for permit processing Appendix III Country-specific listings Export permit from listing country required Check current CITES database for updated listings Non-CITES Racing pigeons (Columba livia domestica), chickens, ducks, most finches No CITES permit Normal shipping documentation sufficient

docs.text: Step Responsible Party Timeline 1. Determine CITES status of species Client / SENO Immediate 2. Obtain export permit from country of origin Client (with SENO support) 4–8 weeks 3. SENO provides letter stating testing purpose SENO 1–2 business days 4. Submit permit applications Client 2–4 weeks processing 5. Ship sample with original CITES permit Client Per permit validity period 6. SENO retains copy of import permit for records SENO At sample arrival

docs.text: Document Purpose Who Prepares Notes Commercial invoice Customs valuation, contents declaration Client (SENO provides template) Declare as "Laboratory Testing Samples, No Commercial Value" Packing list Itemized contents Client Include species, sample type, quantity Letter of explanation Explains samples are for diagnostic testing SENO (provided on request) Use SENO letterhead; states samples will be disposed after testing Health certificate Veterinary clearance (required by some countries) Local veterinarian May need government veterinary authority stamp CITES permit Legal transport of CITES-listed species Country's CITES Management Authority Original required; digital copies not accepted by some customs Airway bill Courier shipping document Courier / Client Use correct UN3373 classification

docs.title: Customs Declaration Best Practices
docs.text:
• Description: "Diagnostic laboratory samples — avian feather/swab/blood — no commercial value"
  • HS Code: 3822.19 (Diagnostic/Laboratory reagents)
  • Value: Declare modest value (≤ $50 USD) for non-commercial samples
  • Quantity: Accurate species and sample count
  • Restricted: Do not declare as "biological waste" or "hazardous material" unless applicable

docs.title: Feather Samples
docs.text:
1. Place feathers in a clean paper envelope
  2. Seal envelope and label with bird ID(s)
  3. Place envelope(s) inside a padded mailer or small box
  4. No special temperature requirements — stable at ambient for > 30 days

docs.title: Swab Samples
docs.text:
1. Ensure swab tubes are sealed tightly
  2. Place in a sealable plastic bag with absorbent material (paper towel)
  3. Use insulated packaging with cold packs for warm-weather shipping (> 30°C ambient)
  4. Mark as "Biological Specimen, Category B" (UN3373)

docs.title: Blood Samples (liquid)
docs.text:
1. Primary container: EDTA tube, sealed with parafilm around cap
  2. Secondary container: Leak-proof tube with absorbent material surrounding primary tube
  3. Outer packaging: Rigid container with cushioning (minimum 2 cm all sides)
  4. Triple packaging required for liquid biological substances per IATA P620

docs.title: FTA Card Samples
docs.text:
1. Allow blood spot to dry completely (minimum 30 min at room temperature)
  2. Place card in original protective sleeve
  3. Seal sleeve in ziplock bag with desiccant pack
  4. No cold chain required; stable for years at ambient temperature

docs.title: Shipping Tips
docs.text:
• Send multiple samples together — reduces per-sample shipping cost
  • Avoid weekend arrivals — Monday–Thursday delivery preferred
  • Declare as "Laboratory Testing Samples, No Commercial Value"
  • Contact SENO first — receive current shipping instructions before sending
  • Use a courier account (DHL/FedEx/UPS) for tracking and insurance
  • Print labels clearly with SENO's full laboratory address and contact phone number

docs.title: Prohibited Shipments
docs.text:
• Samples from CITES Appendix I species without valid export permit
  • Live birds (feathers, swabs, and blood only — no whole animals)
  • Samples in hazardous or leaking containers
  • Samples with insufficient labeling (must include species, sample type, and sender)
  • Samples with visible mold or fungal growth
  • Syringes or sharps without proper sharps container

docs.text:

docs.title: Sample Storage & Stability
docs.text: Proper storage and handling of avian biological samples is critical to preserving DNA integrity and ensuring accurate test results. This document provides detailed stability data, storage guidelines for each sample type, and recommendations for holding periods before extraction or shipment to SENO.

docs.title: General Principles of Sample Preservation
docs.text:
DNA degradation begins immediately after sample collection due to active nucleases released from damaged cells. The goal of proper storage is to slow or halt this degradation. Key factors affecting DNA stability include:

  • Temperature — Lower temperatures slow enzymatic degradation
  • Humidity — Moisture promotes microbial growth and nuclease activity
  • Light exposure — UV light causes DNA crosslinking and fragmentation
  • Time — DNA degrades progressively; earlier extraction yields better results
  • pH and chemical environment — Stabilization buffers (FTA cards, swab solutions) preserve DNA chemically

docs.title: Storage Conditions by Sample Type
docs.text: Sample Type Short-Term Storage (< 2 weeks) Long-Term Storage (> 2 weeks) Critical Notes Freshly plucked feathers Room temp (15–25°C), dark, dry Room temp in dark container Avoid humidity > 60%; mold degrades DNA completely Blood (EDTA tube) 2–8°C (refrigerator) −20°C or −80°C Freeze within 7 days of collection for best recovery Blood (FTA card, dried) Room temp (15–25°C) Room temp with desiccant Stable for years when moisture is excluded Blood (filter paper spot) Room temp (15–25°C) Room temp with desiccant Stable for up to 6 months Swab in stabilization buffer 2–8°C (refrigerator) −20°C Buffer contains nuclease inhibitors Tissue (post-mortem) 2–8°C (refrigerator) −80°C Freeze immediately after collection; avoid freeze-thaw cycles Semen 2–8°C (short term) −80°C Requires specialized cryopreservation buffer

docs.title: DNA Stability Data (SENO Internal Validation)
docs.text:
SENO has conducted extensive internal validation studies to quantify DNA stability across sample types and storage conditions. The following data represents percentage of intact DNA relative to a freshly extracted reference sample.

Storage Condition Sample Type Storage Duration DNA Intact (%) PCR Success Rate Room temp (15–25°C) Feather (freshly plucked) 30 days > 90% > 95% Room temp (15–25°C) Feather (freshly plucked) 90 days > 80% > 90% Room temp (15–25°C) Feather (freshly plucked) 180 days > 60% > 75% Room temp (15–25°C) Blood (FTA card) 30 days > 95% > 98% Room temp (15–25°C) Blood (FTA card) 365 days > 90% > 95% Room temp (15–25°C) Blood (FTA card) 5 years > 80% > 85% 4°C (refrigerator) Blood (EDTA) 3 days > 98% > 99% 4°C (refrigerator) Blood (EDTA) 7 days > 95% > 97% 4°C (refrigerator) Blood (EDTA) 14 days > 85% > 90% −20°C (freezer) Blood (EDTA) 6 months > 90% > 95% −20°C (freezer) Blood (EDTA) 2 years > 80% > 90% −80°C (deep freeze) Tissue 1 year > 90% > 95% −80°C (deep freeze) Tissue 2 years > 85% > 92% Room temp (15–25°C) Swab (stabilized) 14 days > 95% > 97% Room temp (15–25°C) Swab (stabilized) 30 days > 85% > 90% 4°C (refrigerator) Swab (stabilized) 30 days > 95% > 98% −20°C (freezer) Swab (stabilized) 6 months > 90% > 95%

docs.title: Key Takeaways from Stability Data
docs.text:
• FTA cards provide the most robust long-term room-temperature preservation — DNA remains > 80% intact for at least 5 years when stored dry
  • Freshly plucked feathers degrade faster than FTA blood — ship within 2–4 weeks for optimal results
  • EDTA blood degrades significantly after 7 days at 4°C — freeze or extract within the first week
  • Stabilized swab samples maintain excellent integrity for 14 days at room temperature, making them practical for international shipping without cold packs

Shipment Within 48 Hours

docs.title: Effect of Freeze-Thaw Cycles
docs.text:
Repeated freeze-thaw cycles cause mechanical shearing of DNA and activation of residual nucleases. The impact varies by sample type.

Number of Freeze-Thaw Cycles EDTA Blood (4°C/−20°C) Swab (−20°C) Tissue (−80°C) 1 Minimal loss (< 5%) Minimal loss (< 5%) Minimal loss (< 3%) 2 Moderate loss (10–15%) Moderate loss (10–15%) Low loss (< 8%) 3 Significant loss (25–30%) Significant loss (20–25%) Moderate loss (10–15%) 4+ Severe loss (> 40%) Severe loss (> 35%) Significant loss (> 20%)

Recommendation: If long-term storage or multiple analyses are anticipated, aliquot samples into single-use volumes before freezing.

docs.title: Swab Collection Protocol (Disease Testing)
docs.text: Swab samples are the preferred sample type for avian disease testing at SENO. Oral and cloacal swabs are collected using sterile flocked swabs and immediately placed into nucleic acid stabilization buffer to preserve pathogen RNA and DNA for downstream molecular detection.

docs.title: When to Use Swab Samples
docs.text:
Swab-based disease testing is indicated in the following scenarios:

  • Respiratory disease investigation — Oral/choanal swabs for detection of respiratory viruses and bacteria
  • Enteric disease investigation — Cloacal swabs for gastrointestinal pathogen screening
  • Comprehensive health screening — Combined oral + cloacal swabs for full pathogen panel
  • Quarantine or import screening — Pre-movement health clearance testing
  • Outbreak investigation — Rapid collection from multiple birds during disease outbreaks
  • Neonatal testing — Safer than blood collection in very young chicks

docs.title: Swab Type Selection
docs.text: Swab Type Collection Site Target Pathogens Best Use Case Oral swab Oropharynx, choanal slit PiHV, PPMV-1, AIV, NDV, Mycoplasma, Avian Chlamydia Respiratory disease screening Cloacal swab Cloaca PiADV, Salmonella, E. coli, Avian Coronavirus, Enteric viruses Enteric disease screening Combined swab (both sites) Oral + cloacal All pathogens listed above Comprehensive health certification Ocular swab Conjunctiva Mycoplasma, Avian Chlamydia, AIV Ocular infection cases Tracheal swab Trachea AIV, NDV, IBV, Bordetella Deep respiratory sampling

docs.title: Materials Required
docs.text: Item Quantity Notes Sterile flocked swabs 1–2 per bird Flocked swabs collect 3–5× more cells than fiber swabs Nucleic acid stabilization solution 1 tube per swab Provided by SENO; contains nuclease inactivators Sterile gloves 1 pair per bird Change gloves between birds to prevent cross-contamination Sample labels 1 per tube Waterproof, pre-printed or handwritten Biohazard bag 1 per shipment Secondary containment for transport Cold packs As needed For shipments > 48 hours from collection Permanent marker 1 For writing on tube labels

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
1. Put on a fresh pair of sterile gloves
  2. Remove a sterile flocked swab from its packaging (avoid touching the tip)
  3. Open the stabilization buffer tube and set the cap aside (keep clean)

docs.title: Collection Steps
docs.text:
1. Gently restrain the bird — towel restraint is recommended for parrots and other psittacines
  2. Open the beak by applying gentle pressure on the commissures (corners of the mouth)
  3. Insert the swab into the oropharynx — the cavity at the back of the mouth
  4. Rotate the swab against the mucosal surface for 5–10 seconds with gentle pressure
  5. Swab the choanal slit — the narrow opening on the roof of the mouth (palate)
  6. Rotate again for 3–5 seconds against the choanal mucosa
  7. Withdraw the swab carefully — avoid touching the beak, tongue, or outside of the mouth
  8. Place the swab tip into the stabilization buffer tube
  9. Break or cut the swab handle at the break line (most flocked swabs have a pre-scored break point)
  10. Seal the tube tightly — ensure the cap is fully closed to prevent leakage
Step Duration Key Checkpoint Restraint 10–15 seconds Bird must be calm; excessive struggling reduces swab quality Oral swabbing 5–10 seconds Adequate mucosal contact; visible moisture on swab Choanal swabbing 3–5 seconds Swab contacts the slit on the palate Buffer immersion Immediate Delay > 30 seconds may allow DNA/RNA degradation

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
1. Use a fresh pair of sterile gloves (even if collecting oral and cloacal from the same bird)
  2. Remove a new sterile flocked swab from packaging
  3. Open a separate stabilization buffer tube

docs.title: Collection Steps
docs.text:
1. Restrain the bird with the vent (cloacal opening) exposed
  2. Moisten the swab tip with sterile saline or stabilization buffer (optional — reduces friction)
  3. Insert the swab approximately 0.5–1 cm into the cloaca (do not force)
  4. Rotate the swab gently for 3–5 seconds — the swab tip should contact the cloacal mucosa
  5. Withdraw the swab and inspect the tip for visible fecal material (a small amount is expected)
  6. Place the swab tip into the stabilization buffer tube
  7. Break the swab handle at the break line and seal the tube
Parameter Specification Notes Insertion depth 0.5–1.0 cm Do not exceed 1 cm in small birds Rotation time 3–5 seconds Gentle rotation, not aggressive scraping Fecal contamination Expected Small amount acceptable; heavy contamination may inhibit PCR Buffer immersion Immediate Place into buffer within 30 seconds

docs.title: Combined Oral + Cloacal Swab Protocol
docs.text:
For comprehensive disease screening, SENO recommends collecting both an oral and a cloacal swab from each bird. These can be placed into a single stabilization buffer tube (one swab per tube is still acceptable). When combining:

  1. Collect the oral swab first (less contaminated)
  2. Place the oral swab into the stabilization tube and break the handle
  3. Collect the cloacal swab with a fresh swab
  4. Add the cloacal swab to the same tube
  5. Seal the tube and label as "Combined Oral + Cloacal"

docs.title: Stabilization Buffer Handling
docs.text:
The nucleic acid stabilization solution provided by SENO contains chemical agents that:

  • Inactivate cellular and microbial nucleases (RNases and DNases)
  • Precipitate nucleic acids in a protected state
  • Prevent microbial growth during transport
  • Maintain DNA and RNA integrity at ambient temperatures for up to 14 days
Buffer Property Detail Composition Guanidine-based denaturing solution with chelating agents pH 6.5–7.5 (buffered) Color Colorless to pale yellow Storage before use Room temperature (15–25°C) Shelf life (unopened) 24 months from manufacture date Volume per tube 1.5 mL (sufficient for 1–2 swabs)

WARNING: The stabilization buffer contains guanidine salts. Avoid contact with skin and eyes. If contact occurs, rinse with copious amounts of water. Do not ingest. Do not mix with bleach or chlorine-containing disinfectants — toxic gas may be produced.

docs.title: Labeling
docs.text:
Label each tube immediately after collection with the following information using a waterproof marker:

  • Bird ID (or band number)
  • Collection date (YYYY-MM-DD format preferred)
  • Sample type (Oral / Cloacal / Combined)
  • Collector initials

docs.title: Storage Before Shipment
docs.text: Shipping Timeline Storage Condition Notes Within 24 hours 2–8°C (refrigerator) Cold pack recommended for summer shipments Within 48 hours 2–8°C (refrigerator) Acceptable; buffer maintains integrity 2–14 days 2–8°C or −20°C Freeze if > 48 hours for maximum RNA preservation > 14 days −20°C (freezer) RNA integrity declines after 14 days at 4°C

docs.title: Packaging for Shipment
docs.text:
1. Place sealed tubes upright in a tube rack or padded container
  2. Place the rack inside a sealed biohazard bag
  3. Place the biohazard bag inside an insulated box
  4. Add cold packs (conditioned at 4°C) for ambient-temperature shipments
  5. Add dry ice for frozen shipments — declare as UN3373 Biological Substance, Category B
  6. Include the SENO submission form in a waterproof sleeve on top of the cold pack (not frozen)

docs.title: Quality Control Checkpoints
docs.text:
Before sealing the shipment, verify:

  • [ ] Tubes are labeled with bird ID and date
  • [ ] Tubes are sealed tightly (no buffer leakage)
  • [ ] Swab tips fully submerged in stabilization buffer
  • [ ] Gloves changed between each bird
  • [ ] Cold packs are conditioned (not frozen) for refrigerated shipments
  • [ ] Submission form is included and matches labels
  • [ ] Biohazard bag is sealed

docs.title: Species Guides
docs.text: SENO's species-specific testing guides provide tailored recommendations for different bird groups, considering species-specific variations in CHD intron size, sampling techniques, and disease susceptibility.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Not all birds are the same — at least not from a molecular testing perspective. The CHD gene intron varies in size across species, affecting primer set selection and fragment analysis method. Sample types yield different DNA amounts depending on bird size. Disease susceptibility varies dramatically between taxonomic groups — PBFD is a concern in parrots but essentially absent in pigeons, while pigeons carry PiCV and PPMV-1 that are rare in parrots. These differences make species-specific guidance essential for optimal testing outcomes.

SENO's species guides consolidate decades of laboratory experience into practical recommendations organized by taxonomic group.

docs.title: Conservation Breeding Programs
docs.text:
Captive breeding programs for endangered species rely on accurate sex identification for:

  • Sex-ratio management: Ensuring equal representation of males and females in breeding colonies
  • Pair formation: Confirming male-female pairs for genetic management
  • Juvenile sexing: Identifying sex of hatchlings before banding and release
  • Genetic diversity management: Avoiding over-representation of one genetic lineage

SENO supports conservation programs with discounted testing rates for registered conservation breeding facilities. Contact SENO for program details.

What is the bird species?
├─ Psittacine (Parrot, Macaw, Cockatoo, etc.)
│  ├─ Large (>300 g)?  → 3–5 feathers, P2/P8, gel or CE
│  └─ Small (<100 g)?  → 5–7 feathers, P2/P8+2550F/2718R, CE preferred
│  └─ Disease: PBFD + APV recommended
│
├─ Columbiform (Pigeon, Dove)
│  ├─ Racing pigeon?    → 3–5 feathers, P2/P8, gel OK
│  │                    → Add performance genes + disease panel
│  └─ Pet/Fancy?        → 3–5 feathers, P2/P8, gel OK
│  └─ Disease: 11-pathogen panel recommended
│
├─ Passerine (Canary, Finch, Songbird)
│  ├─ Canary?           → 5–7 feathers, P2/P8, gel or CE
│  ├─ Finch?            → 5–7 feathers, P2/P8, CE preferred

│
└─ Other (Poultry, Waterfowl, etc.)

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
Q: Why do small parrots need more feathers than large parrots? A: The feather follicle size scales with the bird. A macaw feather follicle might yield 50–100 ng of genomic DNA, while a budgerigar follicle might yield only 5–15 ng. Since PCR requires a minimum template of ~20 ng per reaction, more small feathers are needed to compensate.

Q: Can I apply parrot recommendations to my lovebird? A: Lovebirds are technically psittacines (parrots), so the small parrot recommendations apply: use 5–7 feathers and consider capillary electrophoresis for fragment analysis as CHD-W and CHD-Z are close in size.

Q: My species is not listed in any of the three guides. Where should I look? A: Check the Species Compatibility Matrix for a complete list. If your species is not listed there, contact SENO for feasibility assessment.

Last updated: August 2026

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Pigeons represent a significant portion of SENO's testing volume, particularly racing pigeons (homing pigeons). SENO processes 600+ performance gene tests and 500+ virus PCR tests from pigeon samples monthly. The pigeon racing industry — particularly strong in Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, Taiwan, China, and the Middle East — drives demand for comprehensive genetic services that go beyond basic DNA sexing.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Columbiformes (pigeons and doves) encompass over 300 species worldwide. The domestic pigeon (Columba livia domestica) was one of the first birds domesticated by humans (~5,000+ years ago), and selective breeding has produced an extraordinary diversity of breeds — from the high-velocity Racing Homer to the flamboyant Fantail and the vocal Trumpeter.

Pigeons differ from psittacines in several important respects for genetic testing:

  • CHD sexing is straightforward: ~25–30 bp fragment size difference means gel separation is reliable
  • Disease profile is distinct: PiCV, PPMV-1, and PiHV are the primary concerns, not PBFD
  • Performance genetics is a major field: Unlike parrots, pigeons have well-studied performance markers
  • Sample size is smaller: 300–500 g body weight makes blood collection safe and easy

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
Q: How early can I sex a racing pigeon? A: From day one. The CHD gene sequence is determined at fertilization — a squab's DNA carries the same sex information as an adult's. No need to wait for behavioral cues or sexual maturity (6–12 months).

Q: Can DNA fingerprinting replace bands/rings? A: No — rings are the primary identification for competition. However, fingerprinting serves as a secondary "genetic ring" that uniquely identifies the bird if a ring is lost, damaged, or swapped.

Q: How is the performance gene test useful if it doesn't predict racing winners? A: The test identifies genetic potential, not racing results. Used over multiple seasons and across a whole loft population, it helps breeders make data-informed pairing decisions — biasing towards combinations of favourable marker alleles that correlate with improved racing performance in population studies.

Q: What is the most common health issue in racing pigeons detected by PCR? A: PiCV (Pigeon Circovirus) is the most frequently detected pathogen in routine screening panels. PiCV causes immunosuppression that predisposes birds to secondary infections with other pathogens. It is particularly common in young birds and often underdiagnosed clinically.

Q: Do you test for Trichomonas? A: Trichomonas (canker) is a protozoal infection rather than a viral/bacterial pathogen, and is not included in SENO's standard 11-pathogen PCR panel. Trichomonas is typically diagnosed by microscopic examination of oral swabs by a veterinarian.

Last updated: August 2026

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: SENO tests a variety of passerine species (songbirds), primarily for DNA sexing applications. Many passerines are sexually monomorphic — males and females share near-identical plumage — making DNA testing the only reliable method for gender identification outside the breeding season when song distinguishes males.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
The passerine order (Passeriformes) is the largest order of birds, containing over 5,000 species — more than half of all bird species. Fringillidae (finches) and Estrildidae (waxbills) are the most commonly tested families, driven by the aviculture and exhibition communities.

Passerines present unique challenges for molecular testing:

  • Small body size: Canaries weigh 15–30 g, finches as little as 10–20 g — limiting blood collection volume
  • Small feather follicles: A canary feather follicle yields 5–15 ng DNA vs. 50–100 ng for a macaw
  • Fragile nature: Stress from handling during sample collection can be dangerous for very small birds
  • CHD fragment resolution: Some species produce CHD-W and CHD-Z fragments that are close in size
  • Disease profile: Different from psittacines — PBFD is not a concern in passerines, but APV and AIV can be

SENO has validated CHD sexing for 50+ passerine species, primarily from Fringillidae, Estrildidae, and Ploceidae families.

docs.title: Sexing by Visual Cues vs. DNA Testing
docs.text:
Species Male Visual Cues Female Visual Cues Accuracy of Visual Sexing Domestic Canary Song (seasonal); vent shape in some varieties Undistinguishable plumage; no sustained song ~80% during breeding; ~50% otherwise Zebra Finch Orange cheek patch, barred chest, chestnut flank Grey plumage, no cheek patch ~95% adult; 0% juvenile Gouldian Finch Brighter colour in all morphs; purple chest Less vivid colour; pale chest ~70% adult; 0% juvenile Society Finch Song (brief, soft); courtship display No song; submissive posture ~60% outside breeding; 0% juvenile Java Sparrow Thicker beak base; courtship song Slightly thinner beak ~60% adult; 0% juvenile Canary (Red Factor) Same as standard canary Same as standard canary ~80% via song; 0% via plumage

Visual sexing accuracy is 0% for juvenile birds of all species — making DNA testing the only option for nestlings and young birds.

docs.title: Feather Collection (Preferred Method)
docs.text:
• Use 5–7 feathers minimum (small follicle = less DNA)
  • Pluck from the chest/breast region — follicles here are richest in DNA
  • Hold the bird in a darkened cloth/Towel (less stressful than open handling)
  • Support the bird's body — pressure on the chest can restrict breathing in birds < 20 g
  • Do not pluck tail feathers: they contain less DNA and take longer to regenerate
  • Inspect each feather base: the follicle should appear white and bulbous; discard if dry

docs.title: Blood Collection
docs.text:
• Maximum 0.05 mL (50 µL) for birds under 15 g; 0.1 mL for birds up to 30 g
  • Use a 27–30G needle for venipuncture (very fine)
  • FTA card blood spots preferred — less stress than EDTA tube collection
  • Apply gentle pressure to puncture site for 10–15 seconds after collection to prevent hematoma
  • A single drop of blood (10–20 µL) on an FTA card is sufficient for both sexing and basic disease PCR

docs.title: What NOT to Do
docs.text: Practice Risk Alternative Buccal swab on small finches Very high failure rate (> 50%) Feathers or FTA blood spot Blood collection > 0.1 mL in canary Anemia, collapse, death Limit to 0.05 mL; use FTA card Plucking wing feathers Painful; may affect flight Chest feathers only Transport without proper cushioning Stress → death Use well-ventilated, dark container

docs.title: CHD Fragment Sizes in Passerines
docs.text:
Species P2/P8 Male (bp) P2/P8 Female (bp) Difference Notes Canary (Serinus canaria) ~375 375 + ~390 ~15 bp Good gel resolution Zebra Finch (T. guttata) ~370 370 + ~385 ~15 bp Good resolution Gouldian Finch (E. gouldiae) ~365 365 + ~380 ~15 bp Good resolution Society Finch (L. domestica) ~370 370 + ~385 ~15 bp Good resolution Java Sparrow (L. oryzivora) ~370 370 + ~385 ~15 bp Good resolution

Most passerine species tested at SENO show a ~15 bp difference between CHD-W and CHD-Z with the P2/P8 primer pair, which is reliably resolvable on a 3% agarose gel or capillary electrophoresis system. The 2550F/2718R primer set serves as backup if co-migration is suspected.

docs.text:
Passerines are generally not susceptible to PBFD (psittacine-specific). Relevant pathogens include:

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
Q: Can I sex a canary by its colour? A: No. Canary colour (yellow, white, red, variegated) is determined by autosomal genes that are not sex-linked. Red Factor canaries are not all male — females also express the red pigment. Colour is a completely unreliable indicator of sex in canaries.

Q: Why is the failure rate higher for finch samples than for parrot samples? A: The primary reason is DNA quantity. A canary feather follicle may contain 10× less DNA than a macaw feather follicle. If the feather is not freshly plucked with an intact follicle, or if an insufficient number is submitted, the extracted DNA may fall below the threshold needed for reliable PCR amplification.

Q: How can I visually estimate the sex of my Gouldian Finch? A: Adult Gouldian Finch males have a brighter purple chest, deeper green back, and more vivid yellow belly than females. However, color intensity varies by individual, and birds less than 6 months old cannot be sexed visually at all. Young Gouldian finches of both sexes look identical. DNA testing is the only reliable method for juveniles.

Q: Do male canaries sing? A: Yes — sustained, complex song is a male characteristic. Female canaries may chirp and make brief calls but do not produce the elaborate song of the male. However, juvenile males don't sing (typically start at 6–10 months), and some males sing only during the breeding season. A non-singing bird cannot be assumed to be female.

Q: Can I test my finch for APV? A: Yes. Avian Polyomavirus can infect finches and canaries, though it is less common than in budgerigars. Testing is recommended if you have unexplained deaths in juvenile finches or are introducing new birds to an existing collection.

Q: Is it safe to pluck feathers from a Gouldian Finch? A: Yes, when done correctly. Gouldian Finches are delicate (14–17 g) but tolerate chest feather plucking if the procedure is quick and the bird is handled gently. Use a soft cloth to hold the bird, pluck only 5–7 chest feathers, and return the bird to its cage immediately. Do not hold for more than 30 seconds. For very nervous birds, consider FTA card blood spot collection instead (requires single drop of blood).

Last updated: August 2026

docs.title: Background
docs.text: Psittacines (order Psittaciformes) encompass over 350 species of parrots, macaws, cockatoos, lorikeets, lovebirds, and budgerigars. They represent the largest group of captive birds tested at SENO, accounting for approximately 55% of all DNA sexing samples and 80% of disease testing samples. Parrots are prominently represented because: (1) many species are sexually monomorphic and require DNA sexing, (2) they are long-lived (20–80+ years) and often kept as companion animals, (3) they are susceptible to several species-specific viral diseases, and (4) the international pet trade and aviculture community demands reliable testing.

docs.title: Small Psittacines (Lovebirds, Budgies, Parrotlets)
docs.text:
• Use 5–7 feathers for DNA extraction (small follicles = limited DNA yield)
  • CHD-W and CHD-Z fragments with P2/P8 may be only 5–10 bp apart
  • Capillary electrophoresis strongly recommended in place of gel-based analysis
  • Disease screening: combined oral/cloacal swab recommended
  • Lower blood volume limits in very small species (≤ 0.1 mL for birds under 50 g)

docs.title: Medium Psittacines (Conures, Cockatiels, Ringnecks, Small Amazons)
docs.text:
• Use 3–5 feathers sufficient for both sexing and disease testing
  • P2/P8 primer pair generally provides adequate separation
  • Gel electrophoresis (2.5–3% agarose) usually sufficient for fragment discrimination
  • Disease screening: separate oral swab for APV/PBFD if clinical signs present

docs.title: Large Psittacines (Macaws, Cockatoos, African Greys)
docs.text:
• 2–3 feathers sufficient for sexing — the follicles are large and DNA-rich
  • Preferred blood volume: 0.3–0.5 mL for disease testing
  • P2/P8 primer pair gives reliable separation (15–25 bp difference typically)
  • PBFD screening recommended for all new arrivals before introducing to collections
  • Regular (quarterly to semi-annual) PBFD testing recommended for multi-bird facilities

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
Q: Do all parrot species need the same primer set? A: Most large and medium parrots work well with P2/P8. Small parrots (budgies, lovebirds, parrotlets) sometimes require the 2550F/2718R alternative primer set because the CHD-W and CHD-Z fragments are very close in size with P2/P8.

Q: Should I test my parrot for PBFD even if it looks healthy? A: Yes, especially if you have multiple birds or plan to introduce the bird to an existing collection. BFDV-infected birds can be asymptomatic carriers, shedding virus intermittently without visible signs. Pre-introduction testing is the only way to identify these carriers.

Q: Can I use the same feather sample for both DNA sexing and disease testing? A: For standard testing, feathers are used for DNA sexing (genomic DNA) and separate swabs are preferred for disease testing (viral DNA/RNA). However, if only feathers are available, the DNA extract can be tested for both purposes if extraction yields sufficient material.

Q: Why is APV more common in budgerigars than in other parrots? A: Budgerigars (Melopsittacus undulatus) are considered the primary natural reservoir of APV. The virus was historically named "Budgerigar Fledgling Disease" due to its high prevalence and mortality in young budgerigars. Other psittacine species can be infected but are generally less susceptible.

docs.title: Testing Methods & Technology
docs.text: SENO employs a comprehensive suite of molecular biology techniques optimized for avian sample types. Our self-developed reagents are designed for the specific challenges of feather and swab samples, including melanin inhibition resistance and low-template (low-copy number) amplification. All methods are validated following CLSI EP guidelines and operate under our ISO 9001:2015 and ISO 13485:2016 certified quality management systems.

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
Q: Which method is best for routine sexing? A: Conventional PCR with P2/P8 primers followed by agarose gel electrophoresis. It is cost-effective, reliable (> 99% concordance with known-sex birds across 50+ species), and requires no specialized instrumentation beyond a thermocycler and gel system.

Q: When should qPCR be used instead of conventional PCR? A: qPCR is preferred when quantification is needed (viral load for disease monitoring), when higher sensitivity is required (detecting early or low-level infections), or when minimizing contamination risk from post-PCR handling is critical (closed-tube detection).

Q: What is capillary electrophoresis used for in avian testing? A: Capillary electrophoresis enables base-pair resolution fragment sizing, which is essential for DNA sexing fragment analysis (distinguishing CHD-W and CHD-Z amplicons that may differ by only 10–30 bp) and microsatellite-based DNA fingerprinting for individual identification and parentage verification.

Q: Does SENO develop its own reagents? A: Yes. SENO designs and manufactures proprietary PCR master mixes, qPCR probe sets, DNA extraction kits, primer panels, and stabilization buffers. These reagents are specifically optimized for avian sample types and are produced in our ISO 13485-certified facility.

Q: Are all methods validated? A: Yes. Every testing method undergoes full CLSI EP-compliant validation before deployment. Validation data — including sensitivity, specificity, precision, and accuracy — is documented and maintained per method. See Accuracy Validation for details.

This page provides an overview of SENO's testing methods portfolio. For detailed protocols and SOPs, refer to the individual method pages and the Quality Control section. For inquiries about method validation data, contact quality@senobio.com.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Capillary electrophoresis (CE) separates DNA fragments by size using an electric field within a narrow, liquid-filled capillary. Unlike traditional agarose gel electrophoresis — which separates fragments by migration through a porous gel matrix — CE passes fragments through a polymer-filled capillary while detecting fluorescently labeled molecules by laser-induced fluorescence as they pass a detection window.

CE provides base-pair resolution of DNA fragments, making it the method of choice for applications that require precise sizing: distinguishing CHD-Z and CHD-W amplicons that may differ by only 10–30 base pairs, and scoring microsatellite alleles for individual DNA fingerprinting and parentage verification.

SENO operates two CE instruments supporting high-throughput processing for sexing, fingerprinting, and research applications. CE analysis is performed on PCR products amplified using fluorescently labeled primers as described in our PCR Technology section.

docs.title: Principle of Operation
docs.text:
CE separates DNA fragments based on their electrophoretic mobility through a sieving polymer. Smaller fragments migrate faster and reach the detector earlier. A laser excites fluorescent dyes attached to the labeled primers, and the emitted fluorescence is recorded by a CCD camera. An internal size standard (labeled with a spectrally distinct dye) is co-injected with each sample, enabling fragment sizing by interpolation.

Component Function Capillary (36–50 cm length, 50 µm ID) Separation channel filled with linear polymer matrix Polymer matrix Sieving medium — separates fragments by size Running buffer Provides electrical continuity (1× or 10× Genetic Analyzer Buffer) Laser (488 nm / 514 nm) Excites fluorescent dyes on labeled primers CCD camera Records fluorescence emission across multiple spectral channels POP-4™ or POP-7™ polymer Commercial sieving polymers optimized for different size ranges

docs.text:
CE provides precise sizing of CHD-W and CHD-Z amplicons, resolving fragments that may appear as a single band on agarose gel. This is particularly valuable for species where the CHD-Z and CHD-W intron lengths are similar.

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
Q: Why use CE instead of agarose gel electrophoresis for sexing? A: CE provides single-base-pair resolution, enabling confident discrimination of CHD-Z and CHD-W fragments that differ by as few as 5–10 bp. Agarose gel can miss small differences, leading to incorrect sex assignment in species where CHD introns are nearly identical in length.

Q: How many microsatellite loci does SENO use for fingerprinting? A: Our standard DNA fingerprinting panel includes 12 microsatellite loci, providing a combined power of discrimination exceeding 0.9999. This means the probability of two unrelated individuals sharing the same profile is less than 1 in 10,000.

Q: What size standard does SENO use? A: We use GeneScan™ 500 LIZ™ (16 fragments from 35 to 500 bp) for most applications. For microsatellites with larger alleles (> 400 bp), we use GeneScan™ 600 LIZ™.

Q: Can CE distinguish between same-sex siblings? A: Yes. While CHD sexing identifies the genetic sex, microsatellite fingerprinting by CE distinguishes individual identity regardless of sex. Same-sex siblings will have different microsatellite profiles (unless they are identical twins, which is extremely rare in birds).

Q: How long does a CE run take? A: For the ABI 3500 (8 capillaries), a full 96-sample run takes approximately 45 minutes. For the SeqStudio Flex (4 capillaries), approximately 60 minutes. Total turnaround including plate preparation and data analysis is about 3–4 hours for 96 samples.

This document describes SENO's capillary electrophoresis methodology and applications. For CE protocol SOPs, refer to the Quality Control section. For questions about fingerprinting applications, contact info@senobio.com.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is a molecular biology technique that amplifies specific DNA sequences from small quantities of starting material. PCR is the foundation of avian DNA testing at SENO. Every testing service — from routine sex determination to pathogen screening and microsatellite genotyping — begins with PCR amplification.

SENO's PCR protocols are specifically optimized for avian samples. Unlike human or mammalian PCR, avian DNA extracted from feather follicles presents unique challenges: low template DNA (often 1–10 ng per reaction), melanin co-purification (a known Taq polymerase inhibitor), and degraded DNA from improperly stored samples. Our protocols address each of these challenges through optimized master mixes, adjusted cycling parameters, and validated primer sets.

docs.title: PCR Process
docs.text:
PCR consists of repeated thermal cycles, each with three main steps that together achieve exponential amplification of the target DNA region. The table below details the typical cycling parameters used at SENO for CHD gene sexing.

Step Temperature Duration Purpose Initial Denaturation 94–95°C 2–5 min Activate polymerase, denature double-stranded template DNA Denaturation (cycle) 94–98°C 15–30 s Separate double-stranded DNA into single strands Annealing (cycle) 50–65°C 15–30 s Allow primers to bind specifically to target sequences Extension (cycle) 72°C 30–60 s/kb Taq DNA polymerase extends new complementary strand Final Extension 72°C 2–5 min Complete all unfinished strands Hold 4°C ∞ Short-term storage of PCR product

Annealing temperature is the most critical parameter for specificity. For P2/P8 primers used in CHD sexing, the optimal annealing temperature is 50°C. A 2–3°C increase improves specificity but may reduce yield; a 2–3°C decrease increases yield but may produce non-specific bands.

docs.title: CHD Gene Sexing
docs.text:
The primary application of conventional PCR at SENO is avian sex determination through amplification of the CHD (Chromo-Helicase-DNA binding) gene. The CHD-Z and CHD-W genes are located on the Z and W sex chromosomes respectively. Conserved primers (P2/P8) amplify an intron region that differs in length between the two genes.

Primer Set Target Forward Sequence (5' → 3') Reverse Sequence (5' → 3') Amplicon Size P2/P8 CHD-Z/W TCTGCATCGCTAAATCCTTT CTCCCAAGGATGAGRAAYTG 350–450 bp 2550F/2718R CHD-Z/W GTTACTGATTCGTCTACGAGA ATTGAAATGATCCAGTGCTTG 600–700 bp
  • Male (ZZ): Single CHD-Z fragment (one band on gel)
  • Female (ZW): CHD-Z + CHD-W fragments (two bands on gel)

In species where the CHD-Z and CHD-W introns are similar in length (producing co-migrating bands), the alternative 2550F/2718R primer set may be used. For example, some Columbiformes (pigeons, doves) and certain Psittaciformes (parrots) show minimal length polymorphism with P2/P8 and require the alternative set.

The detailed protocol for CHD PCR is described in the CHD PCR Protocol SOP.

docs.title: PCR Platform

docs.title: Melanin Inhibition
docs.text:
Feather-derived DNA often contains melanin, a potent inhibitor of Taq DNA polymerase. SENO's protocols mitigate this through:

Strategy Implementation Effect Inhibitor-resistant polymerase Modified Taq with BSA (0.1 µg/µL) Restores activity in melanin presence Extended denaturation Initial denaturation 5 min at 95°C Improved template accessibility Increased polymerase units 0.05 U/µL → 0.1 U/µL Compensates for partial inhibition Additive 3% DMSO or 5% glycerol Reduces secondary structure interference

docs.title: Low Template Amplification
docs.text:

Adjustment Standard Protocol Low-Template Adaptation Template volume 2 µL 4–6 µL Cycles 35 38–40 Extension time 45 s 60 s Primer concentration 0.2 µM 0.3 µM Polymerase units 0.5 U 1.0 U

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Quantitative PCR (qPCR), also known as real-time PCR, monitors DNA amplification in real time using fluorescent signals. Unlike conventional PCR, which detects product only at the end-point (via gel electrophoresis), qPCR captures fluorescence after each cycle, enabling precise quantification of starting template and eliminating the need for post-PCR handling.

At SENO, qPCR is the primary method for disease detection and viral load quantification. Our qPCR assays use both hydrolysis probe (TaqMan) and intercalating dye (SYBR Green) chemistries, depending on the application. All assays are validated following CLSI EP guidelines and run on calibrated real-time PCR instruments.

docs.title: TaqMan (Hydrolysis Probe)
docs.text:
TaqMan probes are sequence-specific oligonucleotides labeled with a fluorophore at the 5' end and a quencher at the 3' end. During amplification, the 5'→3' exonuclease activity of Taq polymerase cleaves the probe, separating the fluorophore from the quencher and generating a fluorescence signal proportional to the amount of target accumulated.

Chemistry Mechanism Specificity Multiplex Capability SENO Application TaqMan probe Probe cleavage by 5' nuclease Target-specific (hybridization required) High (up to 6 channels) Pathogen quantification (PBFD, AIV, APV) SYBR Green Intercalating dye binding to dsDNA Non-specific (melts with any dsDNA) Low (single channel) Sexing verification, melt curve analysis

docs.title: TaqMan Advantages
docs.text: Feature TaqMan SYBR Green Sequence specificity ✓ (probe-dependent) ✗ (dye binds any dsDNA) Multiplex capability ✓ (spectrally distinct dyes) ✗ (single dye) Melt curve analysis ✗ (probe not melt-compatible) ✓ (Tm-based confirmation) Background fluorescence Low Moderate Cost per reaction Higher (~$0.50–1.00/reaction) Lower (~$0.10–0.25/reaction)

docs.title: SENO's TaqMan Multiplex Configuration
docs.text:
SENO's multiplex qPCR assays use up to four spectrally distinct fluorescent channels, enabling simultaneous detection of multiple pathogens or targets in a single reaction.

Channel Dye Excitation (nm) Emission (nm) Typical Target FAM 6-FAM 495 520 BFDV (PBFD) or APV target HEX Hexachlorofluorescein 535 555 Second pathogen target ROX Carboxyrhodamine 585 610 Internal positive control Cy5 Cyanine 5 649 666 Optional third pathogen target

docs.title: qPCR Process
docs.text:
Step Temperature Duration Fluorescence Reading? Initial Denaturation 95°C 3–5 min No Denaturation 95°C 10–15 s No Annealing + Extension + Read 60°C 30–45 s Yes (each cycle) (Optional) Melt Curve 60→95°C, ramp 0.5°C/s ~10 min Yes (continuous) Hold 4°C ∞ —

The annealing/extension step is combined into a single 60°C step for TaqMan assays (using Taq polymerases with fast extension kinetics). For SYBR Green assays requiring melt curve analysis, a post-amplification melt curve ramp is added.

docs.title: Quantification: Ct Values
docs.text:
The cycle threshold (Ct) is the cycle number at which fluorescence exceeds the background threshold. Lower Ct values indicate higher starting target quantity. The relationship between Ct and starting copy number is logarithmic.

Ct Range Interpretation Clinical Meaning < 25 High viral load / strong positive Active infection, high shedding 25–30 Moderate viral load / positive Active infection, moderate shedding 30–35 Low viral load / positive Possible subclinical or early infection 35–38 Very low viral load Equivocal — report as "detected at low level" 38–40 Borderline Suggest retest in 2 weeks No Ct (≥ 40) Negative No target detected

docs.text:

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between qPCR and conventional PCR? A: qPCR measures amplification in real time using fluorescent signals, enabling precise quantification without post-PCR gel analysis. Conventional PCR detects product only at the end-point. qPCR is more sensitive (~10 vs. ~100 copies), faster (1–2 vs. 3–4 hours), and less prone to contamination (closed-tube system).

Q: Why does SENO use TaqMan probes instead of SYBR Green? A: TaqMan probes provide sequence-specific detection, enabling multiplexing (multiple targets in one reaction) and eliminating false positives from primer-dimer or non-specific amplification. SYBR Green is used only for melt curve analysis in specific applications.

Q: How do you interpret a Ct of 36? A: A Ct of 36 indicates very low target levels. The result is reported as "detected at low level" and may suggest subclinical infection, early-stage disease, or residual nucleic acid from a resolved infection. A follow-up sample in 2–4 weeks is recommended to assess trend.

Q: What internal controls are used in qPCR reactions? A: SENO uses a synthetic internal positive control (IPC) added to the master mix (ROX-labeled) and an extraction control (exogenous RNA added during lysis, HEX-labeled). Both must give Ct values within their expected ranges for the reaction to be valid.

Q: How is qPCR quantified? A: A standard curve is generated from serial dilutions of a known-concentration plasmid containing the target sequence. The Ct values of unknown samples are interpolated against this curve to calculate copy numbers. Standard curves are run with each batch or weekly for established assays with stable performance.

This document describes SENO's qPCR methodology and applications. For detailed validation data for specific assays, refer to the Quality Control section. For protocol-specific inquiries, contact quality@senobio.com.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
SENO designs, develops, and manufactures proprietary molecular testing reagents specifically optimized for avian sample types. This in-house reagent program reduces dependency on external commercial suppliers, enables cost-effective testing services, and allows rapid customization of assays for novel species or emerging pathogens.

Our reagent development laboratory is part of the ISO 13485:2016 certified medical device quality management system, meaning our reagents are produced under the same quality standards as commercial in-vitro diagnostic (IVD) kits. The development process follows a structured pipeline from design concept through analytical validation, lot release, and ongoing stability monitoring.

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
Q: Are SENO's reagents compatible with standard laboratory instruments? A: Yes. All reagents are designed for compatibility with common laboratory equipment including standard thermal cyclers (ABI, Bio-Rad), real-time PCR platforms (CFX96, QuantStudio), and capillary electrophoresis instruments (ABI 3500, SeqStudio). No proprietary instrumentation is required.

Q: Does SENO sell reagents to other laboratories? A: Primarily, SENO's reagents are developed for internal use in our testing center's diagnostic services. Custom batches for partner laboratories and reserach collaborations are considered on a case-by-case basis. Contact rd@senobio.com for inquiries.

Q: How does SENO ensure lot-to-lot consistency? A: Every production lot undergoes release testing against a stored reference lot using quantitative activity, specificity, and sensitivity assays. Acceptance criteria require Ct differences ≤ 1.0 cycles and ≥ 95% concordance on clinical samples between the new lot and the reference.

Q: What is the shelf life of SENO's master mixes? A: Liquid PCR master mixes and qPCR probe sets are stable for 12–24 months when stored at −20°C. Stabilization buffers and DNA extraction reagents are stable for 12 months at room temperature. Each lot is labeled with a manufacturing date and expiration date.

Q: Are the reagents optimized for difficult avian samples? A: Yes. This is one of the primary advantages of our in-house development program. Our PCR master mixes contain additives (BSA, DMSO, optimized MgCl₂) that counteract melanin and hemoglobin inhibition commonly encountered in feather and blood samples. Low-template amplification enhancers support detection from as few as 10 copies of target.

Q: Can SENO develop custom primer/probe sets for novel species? A: Yes. The R&D team can develop and validate custom assays for novel species or emerging pathogens. The typical timeline is 4–8 weeks from sequence submission to validated assay, depending on complexity. Contact rd@senobio.com to discuss custom assay development.

This document describes SENO's self-developed reagent program. For reagent performance data, refer to the Accuracy Validation page. For custom development inquiries, contact rd@senobio.com.
